guide:
Each line is one file or folder. Reading a line like
  drwxr-xr-x  2 hari hari 4096 Oct  5 10:00 photos
from left to right:
  d / -       d means a folder, - means a file (l is a shortcut/link)
  rwxr-xr-x   who can read (r), write (w) and run (x) it: first you, then your group, then everyone else
  2           how many links point to it (you can ignore this)
  hari hari   the owner, then the group
  4096        size in bytes (add -h to see KB/MB/GB instead)
  Oct 5 10:00 when it was last changed
  photos      the name
The 'total' line at the top is disk space used, in blocks. Names starting with a dot are hidden files.

Each name is a file or folder in the current folder. Folders are usually shown in blue, programs you can run in green.
Add -l for details (size, date, permissions), and -a to also see hidden files (names that start with a dot).

One line per disk or partition:
  Filesystem  the disk or partition
  Size        how big it is
  Used        how much is taken
  Avail       how much is still free
  Use%        how full it is (worry when it gets above about 90%)
  Mounted on  the folder where you reach it
Your main disk is the one mounted on /. Lines starting with tmpfs or devtmpfs live in memory, not on your disk, so you can ignore them.

Each line is a size, then the file or folder it belongs to (with -h, sizes read like 4.0K, 120M, 2.3G).
To find what's taking up space, add '| sort -h' to put the biggest at the bottom, then cd into the biggest folder and run it again.

Memory (RAM) on the Mem line, swap (disk used as emergency memory) on the Swap line:
  total       all of it
  used        taken by programs
  free        completely unused
  buff/cache  borrowed by Linux to speed things up, given back when programs need it
  available   what programs can actually still use. This is the number to look at.
A small 'free' is normal and fine. A small 'available', or a lot of used swap, means you're low on memory.

One line per running program (process):
  USER     who started it
  PID      its ID number, which is what 'kill <PID>' needs
  %CPU     how much processor it's using right now
  %MEM     how much memory it's using
  VSZ/RSS  memory in KB (RSS is what it really uses)
  STAT     its state: R running, S sleeping (normal), Z zombie (finished but not cleaned up)
  START    when it started
  TIME     total processor time used
  COMMAND  what was run
To find one program: ps aux | grep <name>

Reads as: the time now, how long since the last restart ('up 3 days'), how many people are logged in, and the load average.
The three load numbers are how busy the computer was over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare them with your number of CPU cores ('nproc'): below that number is fine, well above it means things are waiting.

These are this computer's network addresses (IP addresses).
One starting with 192.168., 10. or 172.16-31. is your address on your local network (Wi-Fi or cable). Other devices at home or work can reach you on it, but it's not your public internet address.
Longer ones with colons are IPv6 addresses.

One block per network connection (interface):
  lo        a loopback for the computer to talk to itself (127.0.0.1). Ignore it.
  eth0/enp  a wired connection
  wlan0/wlp a Wi-Fi connection
  UP        connected and on
  inet      the IPv4 address (192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x is your local network address)
  inet6     the IPv6 address

One line per network port in use:
  Netid             tcp or udp
  State             LISTEN means a program is waiting for connections
  Local Address:Port  where it listens
If the address is 127.0.0.1 or [::1], only this computer can connect. 0.0.0.0 or * means other computers can too.
Common ports: 22 SSH, 80 web, 443 secure web, 53 DNS. Add -p (with sudo) to see which program owns each one.

Your disks and their partitions, as a tree:
  NAME        disk names like sda or nvme0n1, partitions like sda1 or nvme0n1p1
  SIZE        how big each one is
  TYPE        disk (the whole drive) or part (a partition of it)
  MOUNTPOINTS the folder you reach it at, if it's in use. / is your main system.
A USB stick usually shows up as a new sdb or sdc when you plug it in.
The number is the count, then the file name. With -l it counts lines, -w words, -c bytes. Without a flag you get all three: lines, words, bytes.

git status sorts your changes into groups:
  Changes to be committed      staged with 'git add'; they go into your next commit
  Changes not staged           edited, but not added yet. Run 'git add <file>' to include them
  Untracked files              new files git isn't watching yet
The first lines say which branch you're on and whether it's ahead of or behind the copy on GitHub (use git push or git pull to sync).

Your project's history, newest first. Each commit shows:
  commit <long id>  its ID (the first 7 characters are enough to refer to it)
  Author            who made it
  Date              when
  the message       what was changed and why
Press q to leave, the arrow keys or space to scroll. 'git log --oneline' gives a short version.
